extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic and philosophy (advanced undergraduates / graduates)
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for analysing the import of propositions, classification of predicates, and criteria for when propositions convey factual information versus merely verbal (definitional) content. Focused on distinguishing five kinds of matters-of-fact, essential vs accidental predication, and the doctrine of the predicables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-fold classification of matters-of-fact asserted in propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every non-verbal proposition asserts (or denies) one of five kinds of matters-of-fact: Existence, Co-existence (Order in Place), Sequence (Order in Time), Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This five-fold division is exhaustive for matters that can be believed or asserted. Examples and discussion show how different propositions fit into these species (e.g., sensory predicates as Resemblance). Use this classification to determine what a proposition actually asserts and therefore what kind of proof or evidence it requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction within Co-existence: Order in Place vs Co-inherence of Attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions of co-existence come in two kinds: (a) propositions of Order in Place (account of place) and (b) co-inherence of attributes — concurrence of two or more attributes or powers in the same part or locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the difference: Order in Place involves spatial arrangement with numerical intervals; co-inherence involves concurrence of attributes (e.g., gold atoms having weight, hardness, color). Co-inherence can be potential rather than actual (e.g., snow is said to be white even in darkness because the color would be perceived in light). Treat co-inherence as a complex case of co-existence, tied to simultaneity and therefore to Time rather than Place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract terms reducible to concrete equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposition expressed in abstract terms can be transformed into a precisely equivalent proposition in which the terms are concrete—either the concrete names that connote the attributes or the names of the fundamenta (facts/phenomena) on which those attributes are grounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To analyze an abstract predication, substitute concrete names for the attribute(s) or the phenomena grounding them (examples: 'Prudence is a virtue' → 'Thoughtless actions are dangerous' → translate to underlying phenomena and classify as one of the five matters-of-fact). This shows that abstract predicates assert Existence, Co-existence, Causation, Sequence, or Resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions merely verbal (verbal propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions that relate only to the meaning of names (conventions of language) and not to matters-of-fact; they are not properly susceptible of truth or falsity but only of conformity to usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such propositions are provable only by evidence of usage; their function is to state meanings/conventions. They include many so-called 'essential' propositions and definitions. Do not treat them as factual claims requiring empirical proof; instead treat proofs as demonstrations of linguistic usage or definitional unpacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential propositions and essential properties
rubrics_metrics.description: An essential proposition predicates an attribute that is part (whole or partial) of what the subject's name connotes (i.e., involved in the meaning of the name). Essential propositions are in fact verbal: they unfold the meaning of the term rather than add information about the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Every man is rational' conveys no new knowledge to one who already understands 'man'. Essential propositions are most useful as Definitions (which should, ideally, unfold the whole connotation). Note: ambiguity of the copula may give the impression that essential propositions imply existence ('A ghost is a disembodied spirit') when in fact they are verbal; be alert to tacit assumptions of real existence when essential propositions are treated as yielding consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental (non-essential) or Real propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions whose predicate connotes an attribute not implied by the subject's name. These are 'real' propositions and, if true, add to our knowledge about the thing rather than merely restating the meaning of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such propositions assert facts about individuals or general properties not contained in the subject's signification (e.g., particular empirical claims). They are the proper subject of informative reasoning and inference; they require appropriate evidence and can serve as premises from which further conclusions follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should unfold connotation (practical standard for good definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete definition should unfold the whole of what is involved in the meaning of the word defined (when the word is connotative). Practically, definitions usually specify enough of the connotation to mark out the objects denoted from other known objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, a definition need not list every connoted attribute; it must provide sufficient marks to distinguish the term's referents. Sometimes an accidental property (not part of the full connotation) serves this distinguishing purpose adequately. Use the distinction between nominal/essential content and pragmatic distinguishing features when drafting or evaluating definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical (evidential/mark) formulation of general propositions for reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When used as memoranda for practical use or as premises in reasoning, general propositions are best expressed as: 'The attributes of X are a mark or evidence of Y'—i.e., one fact is evidence of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation emphasizes how general propositions function in reasoning (to guide expectation in particular cases) rather than merely stating conceptual relations. For purposes of reasoning, treat general propositions as indicating marks/evidence by which one infers or expects other facts (example: 'All men are mortal' = the attributes of man are marks of mortality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the Predicables (five-fold division of general names)
rubrics_metrics.description: General names (predicates) can be classed by the relation they bear to a subject on a particular occasion as one of: genus, species, differentia, proprium, or accidens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are relational categories, not fixed labels of words: the same name may serve as genus with respect to one subject and as species with respect to another (e.g., 'animal' is genus relative to man but species relative to 'being'). Use the predicables to clarify the logical role of a predicate in classification and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification principles: names, attributes, and the creation of classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes are normally constituted by the common attributes connoted by a general name; by introducing a name that connotes particular attributes we (ipso facto) create a class of things that possess those attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that general language often creates classes rather than merely reflecting them; names may be introduced for convenience of classification (e.g., scientific taxa). Regardless of origin, such names are significant only in virtue of the attributes they connote, and good classification for logical inquiry should be grounded in those attributes. The principles regulating classification for inquiry are to be considered further, but keep in view that naming is tied to attributive signification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal essences vs Real essences (Locke's distinction and its logical implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominal essences are the essences of classes (what the name connotes); real essences are supposed properties of individual objects that cause their sensible properties (unknown causes underlying phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's nominal/real distinction matters for demonstration: real essences (if known) would permit demonstration of sensible properties from them. In modern physics, 'real essence' of bodies has tended toward corpuscular structure. When evaluating claims of demonstrative proof, be alert whether the argument depends on nominal (linguistic) connotation or on asserted real essences.
